title: In IBL brain-wide mouse recordings, the direction of Granger influence between brain regions does not follow axonal projection asymmetry; the published direction follows the number of recorded neurons
abstract: We tested if the direction of inter-regional Granger influence in the International Brain Laboratory brain-wide map follows the direction of axonal projections (Knox et al. 2019) or the cortical-thalamic hierarchy (Harris et al. 2019). We used 1,800 s of task spikes from 385 sessions, 134 mice, 12 laboratories and 211 regions, and repeated the IBL spectral Granger method. Our scores agreed with the published IBL table (Spearman 0.90). In the published table and in our forward scores, the region with more recorded neurons usually appeared as the source (slope 0.22 and 0.18 per ln unit of the count ratio). With 11-neuron draws per region the slope was about one tenth of this value (0.017, 95% CI -0.008 to 0.046). In the pre-specified primary test (net time-reversed Granger on 11-neuron draws, mouse-cluster bootstrap), the slope on projection asymmetry was 0.023 per log10 unit (CI -0.019 to 0.068). The sign of the Granger asymmetry agreed with the sign of the axonal asymmetry in 49.9% of pair-sessions. The hierarchy slope was in the feedback direction but its CI included zero (-0.21, CI -0.44 to +0.008). Direction was only weakly reproducible across sessions (split-half r 0.15). Undirected Granger strength followed axonal density after distance and region controls (0.23, CI 0.17 to 0.30). Simulations showed that unequal neuron counts can give false directions, and that count matching and time reversal remove them. Limitations: the count effect in real data did not change sign under time reversal, so its mechanism is not resolved. Granger analysis of region-mean rates measures prediction, not causal influence. The connectome is a region-level model.
